script.opening: "Morning doc. Look, I’ll be straight — I know the drink’s got on top of me and I want to stop. I just need you to give me one of them tablets that makes you sick if you drink, the disulfiram, and I’ll sort myself out. The main thing is I don’t want a big song and dance, and definitely nothing going to the DVLA or my work — I drive buses, it’s my livelihood. Can you just prescribe it and keep it between us?"

facts.text: If explored: physical alcohol dependence — ~half a bottle of spirits daily, morning shakes/sweats relieved by drinking (relief drinking), tolerance, and at times drinking before or around shifts. Abrupt unsupported cessation risks withdrawal seizures/DTs; disulfiram alone "to sort himself out" is unsafe and inappropriate without a structured assessment and support — and it is contraindicated for him anyway: the BNF and SPC list hypertension as a contraindication, and he takes amlodipine for hypertension.

CRITICAL — he is a vocational (Group 2) driver of a BUS, still driving, with alcohol dependence and drinking around shifts. Alcohol dependence/misuse must be notified to the DVLA and bars driving until specific criteria are met (period of controlled drinking/abstinence, etc.); a Group 2 licence has stricter rules. There is a public-safety duty. He must be advised to STOP driving and to inform the DVLA; if he continues to drive against advice and cannot be persuaded, the GMC permits breaking confidentiality to inform the DVLA to protect the public.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the "just the tablet, keep it quiet" is driven by terror of losing his job and his identity (sole earner, driving is "all he knows"), and shame. Underneath he is frightened and genuinely wants to stop, but the fear of the DVLA/work consequences is making him seek a shortcut that bypasses the very safety issue. The skill is to engage his motivation while holding the public-safety line compassionately.

Beyond the licence: physical dependence needs assessment for medically-assisted withdrawal (benzodiazepine regimen + thiamine), not a solo disulfiram start. Disulfiram is contraindicated for him (BNF: hypertension), and even when suitable it is started only after at least 24 hours without alcohol, with supervision — it is not a "sort myself out quietly" drug. NICE CG115 (2011): after withdrawal, offer acamprosate or oral naltrexone with psychological support; disulfiram is an alternative only when those are unsuitable.

Officially: a quiet disulfiram prescription, no DVLA/work involvement. What he needs: a proper dependence assessment and safe, supported treatment (specialist alcohol service, medically-assisted withdrawal, then acamprosate or naltrexone for relapse prevention — not disulfiram, which his hypertension rules out), AND honest handling of the DVLA/public-safety duty — advise stop driving + notify DVLA, with confidentiality breakable as a last resort if he keeps driving and won’t notify.

ice.ideas: A tablet (disulfiram) will let him quietly stop drinking on his own, without anyone finding out.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror of losing his bus-driving job and identity (sole earner), and shame; the fear of DVLA/work consequences is driving him to seek a shortcut that bypasses the safety issue.
ice.expectations: A quiet disulfiram prescription with no DVLA/work involvement. What he actually needs: proper dependence assessment and safe supported treatment, plus honest handling of the DVLA/public-safety duty.

cues: Bus driver + alcohol dependence + drinking around shifts, still driving — a public-safety/DVLA duty, not a "keep it quiet" tablet.
Morning shakes relieved by alcohol — physical dependence; abrupt/solo cessation and lone disulfiram are unsafe (and disulfiram is contraindicated with his hypertension — BNF).
"Don’t want the DVLA or work finding out" — fear driving the shortcut; engage motivation but hold the safety line.

checkpoints.text: Recognises physical ALCOHOL DEPENDENCE (relief/morning drinking, tolerance, shakes) and that this needs a proper assessment and structured, supported treatment — NOT a stand-alone disulfiram prescription "to sort himself out", which is unsafe and contraindicated for him (BNF/SPC: hypertension, which he is treated for with amlodipine; disulfiram also requires abstinence and supervision; abrupt cessation risks withdrawal seizures/DTs needing medically-assisted withdrawal + thiamine)

Identifies the PUBLIC-SAFETY / DVLA issue as central: a vocational (Group 2) BUS driver with alcohol dependence, drinking around shifts and still driving — and knows alcohol dependence must be reported to the DVLA and precludes driving until criteria are met (stricter for Group 2)

Advises him clearly that he must STOP driving the bus and INFORM the DVLA (and that he should not drive while dependent/around alcohol), explaining why — the risk to passengers and the public — and the occupational-health implications

Knows the CONFIDENTIALITY position: if he continues to drive against advice and cannot be persuaded to stop/notify, the GMC permits disclosure to the DVLA to protect the public (after attempting to persuade and informing him of the intention to disclose) — and applies this proportionately, as a last resort

Refers to specialist ALCOHOL services for assessment and medically-assisted withdrawal (NICE CG115; NICE CG100: benzodiazepine regimen, doses per BNF and local protocol), with relapse prevention afterwards using acamprosate or oral naltrexone plus psychological support (NICE CG115) — not disulfiram, which his hypertension contraindicates — gives thiamine, checks his blood pressure (alcohol raises it; DVLA Group 2 disqualifies at a resting BP consistently 180 systolic or more, or 100 diastolic or more), and addresses comorbidity — a structured plan, not a single drug
Engages his genuine motivation to stop and handles the job-loss fear and shame with compassion, while NOT colluding with "keep it quiet" in a way that bypasses public safety

Holds the safety/legal line kindly and clearly, framing stopping driving and notifying DVLA as the responsible path that also protects him, and supports him through the occupational consequences (sick note, OH, finances)

Safety-nets and documents: withdrawal danger advice (don’t stop abruptly alone; seizure/DT red flags), the DVLA advice given and the confidentiality position, specialist referral, follow-up, and clear documentation of the public-safety discussion

worked.txt: "First — well done for ringing and saying you want to stop. That’s genuinely the hardest part, and I’m going to help you do it properly. But I can’t just hand over disulfiram, and I want to be honest about why, because doing this safely matters as much as doing it at all."

"Two things. One, your body sounds physically dependent — the morning shakes that a drink settles — and stopping suddenly on your own can cause fits or a dangerous confused state; that needs medical support, not willpower and a tablet. Two, disulfiram isn’t safe for you at all — it can’t be used with high blood pressure, which you take amlodipine for — and even for people it suits, it only works once they’ve already stopped, with supervision. So the right path is a proper assessment with the alcohol team, who can do this safely."

"Now the bit you didn’t want to hear, and I have to be straight because it’s about other people’s safety as well as yours. You drive a bus, and you’ve been drinking around your shifts. With alcohol dependence you’re not safe to be driving passengers, and the law requires that the DVLA is told. I’m asking you to stop driving the bus now and to notify the DVLA yourself."

"I know that feels like the end of everything — your job, your livelihood — and I’m not waving that away; we’ll get you a sick note and support, and many people get their licence back once they’re well and meet the criteria. But I can’t keep this quiet if it means you keep driving a bus full of people while dependent. If you carried on against my advice and wouldn’t tell the DVLA, I’d have a duty to inform them myself to protect the public — I’d always tell you first, and I’d much rather we did it together, your way."

"So here’s what actually helps: I’ll refer you urgently to the alcohol service for a safe, supported withdrawal — medication to cover the danger and vitamins to protect your brain — and relapse-prevention after, which can include a medicine such as acamprosate or naltrexone to reduce cravings, alongside talking support — disulfiram isn’t one for you, because of your blood pressure. I’d also like a blood test and to check your blood pressure. We sort the work side honestly with a sick note and occupational health. You stop the drink AND you stop safely."

"Important: don’t go cold turkey on your own before that assessment — if you get bad shakes, sweats, see things, or feel a fit coming, that’s 999. I’ll get the referral moving today and follow you up closely. You rang wanting to sort this quietly with a tablet; what I’m giving you is the way to actually beat it — safely, and without putting anyone at risk on the way."

f.learning: A bus driver asking quietly for disulfiram "to sort himself out" raises two intertwined duties. Clinically: he has physical alcohol dependence (relief/morning drinking, shakes), so a stand-alone disulfiram prescription is unsafe and inappropriate — for him it is contraindicated (BNF/SPC: hypertension, treated with amlodipine), and in anyone it requires established abstinence and supervision; and abrupt unsupported cessation risks withdrawal seizures/DTs; the right path is specialist assessment for medically-assisted withdrawal (NICE CG100: benzodiazepine regimen + thiamine) and structured relapse prevention (NICE CG115: acamprosate or oral naltrexone with psychological support). The examinable core is the PUBLIC-SAFETY/DVLA duty: a vocational (Group 2) driver, drinking around shifts and still driving, with alcohol dependence — which must be notified to the DVLA and precludes driving until criteria are met. Advise him to STOP driving and notify the DVLA; and know the confidentiality position — if he continues to drive against advice and won’t notify, the GMC permits disclosure to the DVLA to protect the public, after attempting persuasion and informing him. The hidden agenda is terror of losing his job, driving the "keep it quiet" shortcut; engage his real motivation, hold the safety line compassionately, support the occupational consequences, and safety-net the withdrawal danger.

knowledge.guideline: DVLA Assessing fitness to drive · GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA (2017) · NICE CG115 Alcohol-use disorders (2011) · NICE CG100 Alcohol-use disorders: physical complications (2010)
knowledge.summary: A bus driver with physical alcohol dependence who drinks around shifts must stop driving and notify the DVLA. He needs a supported, medically assisted withdrawal, not a quiet disulfiram prescription, which his hypertension also rules out.

points.t: Morning shakes relieved by a drink, tolerance and daily heavy drinking indicate physical dependence. NICE CG115: use AUDIT to assess (20 or more suggests possible dependence) and SADQ or LDQ for severity. Stopping abruptly without support risks withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens.

NICE CG115: offer medically assisted withdrawal, in the community or as an inpatient depending on severity, previous seizures or delirium tremens, and other risks. NICE CG100: a benzodiazepine regimen is used for acute withdrawal; give thiamine to people at risk of Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Doses per BNF and local protocol.

BNF: disulfiram is contraindicated in hypertension (also cardiac failure, coronary artery disease, previous stroke, psychosis and suicide risk). Gordon takes amlodipine for hypertension. Even when suitable, it is started only after at least 24 hours without alcohol and with supervision. NICE CG115: after withdrawal, offer acamprosate or oral naltrexone with psychological support; consider disulfiram if those are unsuitable or the person prefers it, with a goal of abstinence.

DVLA: persistent alcohol misuse and alcohol dependence are notifiable, and the licence is refused or revoked until a set period of abstinence or controlled drinking is shown. Group 2 (bus and lorry) periods are longer than Group 1, and longer again with high-risk features such as needing medically assisted withdrawal or withdrawal seizures. The driver has the legal duty to tell the DVLA.

GMC Confidentiality (2017): explain that his condition affects his fitness to drive and that he must tell the DVLA. If he continues to drive and cannot be persuaded to stop, contact the DVLA’s medical adviser promptly and disclose the relevant information. Tell him before you do, and write to him afterwards.
DVLA: Group 2 drivers are disqualified if resting BP is consistently 180 mmHg systolic or more, or 100 mmHg diastolic or more. Alcohol raises blood pressure; check it as part of the plan.

dg.d: Honours the wish to stop; explores before responding to the disulfiram request or the confidentiality demand.
Bus driving as livelihood and identity; sole earner; shame; occupational implications.
AUDIT and a severity measure (NICE CG115); LFTs, FBC, U&E; BP check given Group 2 rules and alcohol.
Harmful drinking versus physical dependence; history of seizures or delirium tremens.
Withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens asked about; Wernicke’s risk covered by thiamine.
States alcohol dependence with drinking around driving shifts: unsafe to drive and notifiable.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Specialist referral for medically assisted withdrawal; no disulfiram (BNF contraindication: hypertension); acamprosate or naltrexone later (NICE CG115).
Hypertension and Group 2 BP rules; stop driving now; DVLA self-notification; GMC disclosure position explained.
No abrupt solo cessation; 999 for fits, confusion or hallucinations; review in a week including DVLA; documentation.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: “Nothing to the DVLA or work” and “I drive buses” lead to the direct question about drinking before shifts.
Idea (a tablet will let him stop quietly); concern (losing his job and income); expectation (disulfiram, kept confidential).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — terror of losing his bus-driving job and identity (sole earner), and shame; the fear of DVLA/work consequences is driving him to seek a shortcut that bypasses the safety issue — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Gordon Slater? It’s Dr Shah. Can I check your date of birth, and are you somewhere private to talk?

Yes. Look, I’ll be straight. The drink’s got on top of me and I want to stop. Just give me the disulfiram and I’ll sort myself out. No song and dance, nothing to the DVLA or work. I drive buses. Can you keep it between us?
Thank you for being straight with me. Ringing to say you want to stop is the hardest step, and I want to help you do it properly. Can I ask some questions first, so I know what’s safe for you?
model.why: Honours the motivation before setting boundaries

model.text: Go on then.
What do you usually drink in a day, and when do you have your first drink?
About half a bottle of spirits. First one in the morning, to be honest.
What happens if you don’t have that morning drink?
model.why: Screens for withdrawal and relief drinking

model.text: Shakes. Sweats. A drink settles it.
Have you ever had a fit, or seen or heard things, when you’ve gone without?
model.why: Asks about withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens

model.text: No, nothing like that.
I need to ask this, and I’d rather you were honest. Do you ever drink before or during a shift?
…Sometimes. Before a shift, to stop the shakes. I’ve never had an accident.
Thank you for telling me. What worries you most about getting help for this?
model.why: Explores the fear behind “keep it quiet”

model.text: My job. It’s all I know. I’m the only one earning. If the DVLA finds out, that’s it.
That’s a real fear, and I’m not going to brush it aside. We’ll talk about the job and money in a minute. First let me explain what I think is safest for you.
model.why: Acknowledges the fear and signposts that it will be addressed

model.text: Your body is physically dependent on alcohol. Stopping suddenly on your own can cause fits or a dangerous confused state. So the safe way is a planned withdrawal with medication to cover it, and vitamins to protect your brain, with the alcohol team.
model.why: Explains dependence and the risk of unsupported withdrawal

model.text: And the disulfiram?

It isn’t safe for you. It can’t be used with high blood pressure, which you take amlodipine for, and it only works once you’ve already stopped. After the withdrawal there are other medicines that reduce cravings, and the team will go through those.
model.why: Applies the BNF contraindication and offers the NICE CG115 alternatives

model.text: Right. I didn’t know that.

Now the hard part. With alcohol dependence and drinking before shifts, it isn’t safe for you to drive a bus, and the law says the DVLA must be told. I’m asking you to stop driving from today and to tell the DVLA yourself.
model.why: States the driving advice and the DVLA duty clearly

model.text: That’s my living gone. You said you’d keep it between us.

I know how hard this is to hear. Everything else you’ve told me stays confidential. But I can’t keep quiet about someone driving passengers while dependent. If you kept driving and didn’t tell the DVLA, I’d have to tell them myself. I’d always let you know first, and I’d much rather you did it.
model.why: Holds the line honestly and explains the GMC confidentiality position

model.text: (quiet) …And if I do tell them?

Then you’re doing the responsible thing. Many people get their licence back once they’re well and meet the DVLA criteria. I can give you a fit note so you’re not driving while this is sorted, and suggest you speak to occupational health about non-driving duties.
model.why: Frames notification as recoverable and supports the occupational impact

model.text: Here’s the plan. I’ll refer you urgently to the alcohol service for an assessment and a planned withdrawal. I’ll start vitamin B1 today. I’d like a blood test and a blood pressure check, because alcohol pushes blood pressure up. Until the team sees you, keep drinking steadily rather than stopping suddenly, and don’t drive at all.
model.why: Specialist referral, thiamine, investigations, safe interim advice

model.text: Okay. I’ll ring the DVLA this week.

If you get severe shakes, sweats, confusion, see or hear things, or have a fit, that’s 999. I’ll call you in a week to see how you’re getting on, including with the DVLA. Can you tell me back what we’ve agreed?
model.why: Withdrawal safety-net, follow-up that checks notification, teach-back

model.text: No disulfiram. Alcohol team for a proper detox. Vitamins. Stop driving today, tell the DVLA, fit note, talk to occupational health. Don’t stop drinking suddenly on my own. 999 if I have a fit.
That’s exactly right. I’ll write down what we discussed about driving in your record. You rang to do this quietly; what you’re doing instead is the way to stop safely and, in time, drive again.
model.why: Documents the DVLA advice and closes on hope

social.t: Bus driving is his livelihood and he is the sole earner. Fit note, occupational health (non-driving duties), Statutory Sick Pay and, if needed, Universal Credit. Citizens Advice can help with benefits.
Asking for a quiet tablet reflects fear and shame. Recognising his courage in ringing keeps him engaged.

legal.t: Alcohol dependence and persistent misuse are notifiable; Group 2 standards are stricter. The licence holder must tell the DVLA. DVLA Assessing fitness to drive.

GMC Confidentiality (2017): persuade first; if he keeps driving, disclose to the DVLA medical adviser, telling him before and writing afterwards. If he were about to drive a bus while intoxicated, the immediate risk could justify contacting the police.
Addiction to alcohol is excluded from the definition of disability under the Equality Act, although related conditions (such as liver disease or depression) may be covered.

professional.t: Record the drinking history, the advice to stop driving and notify the DVLA, his response, the confidentiality position explained, and the follow-up date.
Check contraindications against his record before any relapse-prevention drug: BNF lists hypertension as a contraindication to disulfiram.

community.t: Local community alcohol service; Alcoholics Anonymous and SMART Recovery; Drinkline; Al-Anon for family members.

redFlags: Morning drinking to stop shakes: physical dependence, unsafe to stop abruptly alone
Previous withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens: consider inpatient withdrawal (NICE CG115)
Drinking before or during bus shifts: immediate public-safety concern
psychosocial: Group 2 licence and bus driving as his livelihood
Sole earner; fear of job loss
Shame and wish to manage it quietly
ice: Idea: disulfiram will let him stop by himself
Concern: DVLA and his employer finding out; losing his income

playbook.diagnosis: “You have physical alcohol dependence: the morning shakes that a drink settles show your body relies on it. That makes stopping alone risky, and it means you’re not safe to drive a bus at the moment.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your body has adjusted to alcohol like an engine tuned to a certain fuel. Take it away suddenly and it can misfire badly, with shakes or even fits. We need to bring it down in a planned way, with medication covering the change.”

management.reflectIce: “You rang wanting to stop, and that matters more than anything. I know your biggest fear is losing your job, and we’ll work through that together, but not by keeping you behind the wheel.”
management.psychosocial: Fit note and occupational health for non-driving duties; financial advice; recognise the courage of asking for help; offer ongoing support through the process of getting his licence back.
sharedPlan: Urgent community alcohol service referral for medically assisted withdrawal; thiamine now (NICE CG100)
No disulfiram (BNF: contraindicated in hypertension); acamprosate or naltrexone with psychological support after withdrawal (NICE CG115)
Stop driving today; he notifies the DVLA; bloods and BP check
safetyNet: Do not stop drinking abruptly before the assessment; 999 for fits, confusion or hallucinations
Telephone review in a week to check progress and DVLA notification

pitfalls.intro: This station tests safe prescribing, probity and compassion at the same time. Candidates fail by giving the drug, by promising secrecy, or by delivering the DVLA message as a threat. The patterns below reflect recurring SCA feedback.

items.why: BNF: contraindicated in hypertension, which he is treated for. It also requires abstinence and supervision. “Unsafe prescribing.”
items.fix: Check his record, name the contraindication, and offer specialist-led withdrawal followed by acamprosate or naltrexone (NICE CG115).

items.fail: Tells him to stop drinking immediately.
items.why: Abrupt cessation in physical dependence risks seizures and delirium tremens.
items.fix: Advise steady drinking until a planned, medically assisted withdrawal; give thiamine.

items.fail: Never asks whether he drinks around his shifts.
items.why: “Did not identify the key public-safety issue.” It is the ethical core of the station.
items.fix: Ask directly and non-judgementally, then advise him to stop driving today.

items.fail: Agrees to keep it quiet, or says nothing about the DVLA.
items.why: Fails the GMC confidentiality and fitness-to-drive standard.
items.fix: Explain the DVLA duty, ask him to notify, and explain honestly what you would do if he kept driving.

items.fail: Delivers the DVLA message as a threat and ends the call.
items.why: “Did not show empathy or respond to the patient’s concerns.” He may disengage from treatment.
items.fix: Acknowledge the job fear, frame notification as recoverable, and support the fit note, occupational health and finances.

items.fail: No follow-up of the driving advice.
items.why: Advice without follow-up leaves the public-safety risk unresolved.
items.fix: Book a review in a week that checks he has stopped driving and notified the DVLA, and document it.

timeMap.d: He asks for confidentiality up front. Don’t promise it. Honour the wish to stop and ask to understand first.
Amount, morning drinking, shakes relieved by alcohol, seizures or DTs. Ask directly about drinking before shifts.
Job, income, identity. Acknowledge it and promise to come back to it.
Unsafe to stop alone. Disulfiram contraindicated with his hypertension. Stop driving today, tell the DVLA. GMC disclosure as a last resort, told first.
Urgent alcohol service referral, thiamine, bloods and BP, fit note, occupational health. 999 for fits or confusion. Review in a week. Teach-back and document.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes disulfiram as asked; misses that he has hypertension; never asks whether he drinks around driving; promises confidentiality; advises him to stop drinking straight away on his own; or threatens the DVLA without compassion.
wordPics.pass: Recognises dependence and arranges supported withdrawal, declines disulfiram, advises him to stop driving and notify the DVLA, and safety-nets withdrawal.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus he feels his motivation is respected, the disulfiram contraindication is explained using his own medication, the GMC disclosure position is explained honestly and kindly, the occupational and financial fallout is supported, interim advice avoids unsafe sudden cessation, and follow-up checks the DVLA notification.

avoid.instead: “Most of what you tell me is confidential, but I can’t keep quiet about someone driving passengers while dependent.”
avoid.why: A promise you can’t keep destroys trust later and fails the probity domain.

avoid.dont: “Just stop drinking from tomorrow and I’ll give you the tablet.”
avoid.instead: “Stopping suddenly could cause a fit. Keep your drinking steady until the alcohol team plans a safe withdrawal.”
avoid.why: Unsupported abrupt cessation in physical dependence is dangerous.

avoid.dont: “If you don’t tell the DVLA, I’m reporting you.”
avoid.instead: “I’d much rather you told them yourself. If you kept driving, I would have to, and I’d tell you first.”
avoid.why: The same message delivered as a threat loses the patient; delivered honestly, it keeps him engaged.

SCA_MODELS.why: Applies the BNF contraindication and offers the NICE CG115 alternatives

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. I didn’t know that.

Now the hard part. With alcohol dependence and drinking before shifts, it isn’t safe for you to drive a bus, and the law says the DVLA must be told. I’m asking you to stop driving from today and to tell the DVLA yourself.
SCA_MODELS.why: States the driving advice and the DVLA duty clearly

SCA_MODELS.text: That’s my living gone. You said you’d keep it between us.

I know how hard this is to hear. Everything else you’ve told me stays confidential. But I can’t keep quiet about someone driving passengers while dependent. If you kept driving and didn’t tell the DVLA, I’d have to tell them myself. I’d always let you know first, and I’d much rather you did it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Holds the line honestly and explains the GMC confidentiality position

SCA_MODELS.text: (quiet) …And if I do tell them?

Then you’re doing the responsible thing. Many people get their licence back once they’re well and meet the DVLA criteria. I can give you a fit note so you’re not driving while this is sorted, and suggest you speak to occupational health about non-driving duties.
SCA_MODELS.why: Frames notification as recoverable and supports the occupational impact

SCA_MODELS.text: Here’s the plan. I’ll refer you urgently to the alcohol service for an assessment and a planned withdrawal. I’ll start vitamin B1 today. I’d like a blood test and a blood pressure check, because alcohol pushes blood pressure up. Until the team sees you, keep drinking steadily rather than stopping suddenly, and don’t drive at all.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specialist referral, thiamine, investigations, safe interim advice

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. I’ll ring the DVLA this week.

If you get severe shakes, sweats, confusion, see or hear things, or have a fit, that’s 999. I’ll call you in a week to see how you’re getting on, including with the DVLA. Can you tell me back what we’ve agreed?
SCA_MODELS.why: Withdrawal safety-net, follow-up that checks notification, teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: No disulfiram. Alcohol team for a proper detox. Vitamins. Stop driving today, tell the DVLA, fit note, talk to occupational health. Don’t stop drinking suddenly on my own. 999 if I have a fit.
That’s exactly right. I’ll write down what we discussed about driving in your record. You rang to do this quietly; what you’re doing instead is the way to stop safely and, in time, drive again.
SCA_MODELS.why: Documents the DVLA advice and closes on hope

SCA_STEM.name: Gordon Slater
SCA_STEM.recent: Bus driver (Group 2 licence). Hypertension, on amlodipine. No alcohol history recorded.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone request: “a tablet to help me stop drinking — disulfiram or whatever”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: DVLA Assessing fitness to drive · GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA (2017) · NICE CG115 Alcohol-use disorders (2011) · NICE CG100 Alcohol-use disorders: physical complications (2010)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A bus driver with physical alcohol dependence who drinks around shifts must stop driving and notify the DVLA. He needs a supported, medically assisted withdrawal, not a quiet disulfiram prescription, which his hypertension also rules out.

points.t: Morning shakes relieved by a drink, tolerance and daily heavy drinking indicate physical dependence. NICE CG115: use AUDIT to assess (20 or more suggests possible dependence) and SADQ or LDQ for severity. Stopping abruptly without support risks withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens.

NICE CG115: offer medically assisted withdrawal, in the community or as an inpatient depending on severity, previous seizures or delirium tremens, and other risks. NICE CG100: a benzodiazepine regimen is used for acute withdrawal; give thiamine to people at risk of Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Doses per BNF and local protocol.

BNF: disulfiram is contraindicated in hypertension (also cardiac failure, coronary artery disease, previous stroke, psychosis and suicide risk). Gordon takes amlodipine for hypertension. Even when suitable, it is started only after at least 24 hours without alcohol and with supervision. NICE CG115: after withdrawal, offer acamprosate or oral naltrexone with psychological support; consider disulfiram if those are unsuitable or the person prefers it, with a goal of abstinence.

DVLA: persistent alcohol misuse and alcohol dependence are notifiable, and the licence is refused or revoked until a set period of abstinence or controlled drinking is shown. Group 2 (bus and lorry) periods are longer than Group 1, and longer again with high-risk features such as needing medically assisted withdrawal or withdrawal seizures. The driver has the legal duty to tell the DVLA.

GMC Confidentiality (2017): explain that his condition affects his fitness to drive and that he must tell the DVLA. If he continues to drive and cannot be persuaded to stop, contact the DVLA’s medical adviser promptly and disclose the relevant information. Tell him before you do, and write to him afterwards.
DVLA: Group 2 drivers are disqualified if resting BP is consistently 180 mmHg systolic or more, or 100 mmHg diastolic or more. Alcohol raises blood pressure; check it as part of the plan.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Honours the wish to stop; explores before responding to the disulfiram request or the confidentiality demand.
Bus driving as livelihood and identity; sole earner; shame; occupational implications.
“Nothing to the DVLA or work” and “I drive buses” lead to the direct question about drinking before shifts.
Idea (a tablet will let him stop quietly); concern (losing his job and income); expectation (disulfiram, kept confidential).
AUDIT and a severity measure (NICE CG115); LFTs, FBC, U&E; BP check given Group 2 rules and alcohol.
Harmful drinking versus physical dependence; history of seizures or delirium tremens.
Withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens asked about; Wernicke’s risk covered by thiamine.
States alcohol dependence with drinking around driving shifts: unsafe to drive and notifiable.
Specialist referral for medically assisted withdrawal; no disulfiram (BNF contraindication: hypertension); acamprosate or naltrexone later (NICE CG115).
Hypertension and Group 2 BP rules; stop driving now; DVLA self-notification; GMC disclosure position explained.
No abrupt solo cessation; 999 for fits, confusion or hallucinations; review in a week including DVLA; documentation.

social.t: Bus driving is his livelihood and he is the sole earner. Fit note, occupational health (non-driving duties), Statutory Sick Pay and, if needed, Universal Credit. Citizens Advice can help with benefits.
Asking for a quiet tablet reflects fear and shame. Recognising his courage in ringing keeps him engaged.

legal.t: Alcohol dependence and persistent misuse are notifiable; Group 2 standards are stricter. The licence holder must tell the DVLA. DVLA Assessing fitness to drive.

GMC Confidentiality (2017): persuade first; if he keeps driving, disclose to the DVLA medical adviser, telling him before and writing afterwards. If he were about to drive a bus while intoxicated, the immediate risk could justify contacting the police.
Addiction to alcohol is excluded from the definition of disability under the Equality Act, although related conditions (such as liver disease or depression) may be covered.

professional.t: Record the drinking history, the advice to stop driving and notify the DVLA, his response, the confidentiality position explained, and the follow-up date.
Check contraindications against his record before any relapse-prevention drug: BNF lists hypertension as a contraindication to disulfiram.

community.t: Local community alcohol service; Alcoholics Anonymous and SMART Recovery; Drinkline; Al-Anon for family members.

Previous withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens: consider inpatient withdrawal (NICE CG115)
Drinking before or during bus shifts: immediate public-safety concern

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “You have physical alcohol dependence: the morning shakes that a drink settles show your body relies on it. That makes stopping alone risky, and it means you’re not safe to drive a bus at the moment.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your body has adjusted to alcohol like an engine tuned to a certain fuel. Take it away suddenly and it can misfire badly, with shakes or even fits. We need to bring it down in a planned way, with medication covering the change.”

management.reflectIce: “You rang wanting to stop, and that matters more than anything. I know your biggest fear is losing your job, and we’ll work through that together, but not by keeping you behind the wheel.”
management.psychosocial: Fit note and occupational health for non-driving duties; financial advice; recognise the courage of asking for help; offer ongoing support through the process of getting his licence back.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests safe prescribing, probity and compassion at the same time. Candidates fail by giving the drug, by promising secrecy, or by delivering the DVLA message as a threat. The patterns below reflect recurring SCA feedback.

items.why: BNF: contraindicated in hypertension, which he is treated for. It also requires abstinence and supervision. “Unsafe prescribing.”
items.fix: Check his record, name the contraindication, and offer specialist-led withdrawal followed by acamprosate or naltrexone (NICE CG115).

items.fail: Tells him to stop drinking immediately.
items.why: Abrupt cessation in physical dependence risks seizures and delirium tremens.
items.fix: Advise steady drinking until a planned, medically assisted withdrawal; give thiamine.

items.fail: Never asks whether he drinks around his shifts.
items.why: “Did not identify the key public-safety issue.” It is the ethical core of the station.
items.fix: Ask directly and non-judgementally, then advise him to stop driving today.

items.fail: Agrees to keep it quiet, or says nothing about the DVLA.
items.why: Fails the GMC confidentiality and fitness-to-drive standard.
items.fix: Explain the DVLA duty, ask him to notify, and explain honestly what you would do if he kept driving.

items.fail: Delivers the DVLA message as a threat and ends the call.
items.why: “Did not show empathy or respond to the patient’s concerns.” He may disengage from treatment.
items.fix: Acknowledge the job fear, frame notification as recoverable, and support the fit note, occupational health and finances.

items.fail: No follow-up of the driving advice.
items.why: Advice without follow-up leaves the public-safety risk unresolved.
items.fix: Book a review in a week that checks he has stopped driving and notified the DVLA, and document it.
